candidates.label: Konya (ancient Iconium)
candidates.support: The modern city of Konya overlies ancient Iconium continuously; the identification is undisputed and Pleiades and Wikidata's coordinates for the site agree closely.

summary.text: Iconium was a city of Lycaonia (later administratively linked with Galatia) that Paul and Barnabas visited on the first missionary journey, preaching in its synagogue before opposition drove them on to Lystra.

history.text: Ancient writers disagreed on whether Iconium belonged to Phrygia or Lycaonia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that most ancient authorities, among them the Roman orator Cicero, the Greek geographer Strabo and the Roman writer Pliny, wrote from the standpoint of Roman provincial administration and put Iconium in Lycaonia. The Greek historian Xenophon, however, calls it 'the last city of Phrygia', and Acts 14:6 implies the same when Paul and Barnabas flee from Iconium to 'the cities of Lycaonia,' Lystra and Derbe. The same source concludes that in the apostolic period Iconium was a leading city in the south of Galatia, the Roman province, and probably belonged to the region of Phrygia that Acts 16:6 names. Either way it lay in the province of Galatia, which this project gives as its parent.

scripture.textWEB: But they shook off the dust of their feet against them, and came to Iconium.
In Iconium, they entered together into the synagogue of the Jews, and so spoke that a great multitude both of Jews and of Greeks believed.
But some Jews from Antioch and Iconium came there, and having persuaded the multitudes, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead.
When they had preached the Good News to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch,
The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium gave a good testimony about him.
persecutions, and sufferings—those things that happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. I endured those persecutions. The Lord delivered me out of them all.

politicalHistory.note: Includes Pisidia, Lycaonia (the western part) and Paphlagonia, which had already joined the province of Galatia (Pisidia and Lycaonia in 25 BC on King Amyntas's death; Paphlagonia in 6 BC) before 4 BC. The emperor Vespasian detached most of Pisidia to the new province of Lycia and Pamphylia in AD 74; no source describing exactly where that internal line ran was found, so this area is kept whole rather than guessing at a split. Galatia and Cappadocia may have shared one governor from about AD 69 (see the Cappadocia area's own note), though no ancient source states a merger outright, so they stay two areas with their own holders.
